title: POC: NAT failover and DNS anchoring for hybrid private inference
content:
Purpose:

Quick working notes for a customer POC exploring a resilient egress path and deterministic DNS anchoring when running Redwood Private in a hybrid/VPC environment. Goal: ensure predictable outbound behavior (fixed IPs for allowlists), low-latency access to Redwood control plane endpoints, and robust failover without leaking private DNS resolution.

Context / customer constraints:
- Customer: regulated fintech, must restrict outbound to a small set of IPs and use private hosted zones for internal service discovery.
- Requirement: support on-prem and cloud worker pools with single-hop access to inference endpoints.
- No internet egress allowed from model-serving subnets except through an approved egress appliance/stack.
- Must integrate with customer KMS for key wrapping of credentials and use customer-managed DNS for service names.

High-level acceptance criteria for POC:
- Demonstrate deterministic egress IPs for Redwood control plane and model pull endpoints (NAT failover).
- Show split-horizon DNS where internal names resolve to private endpoints and external names resolve to public control plane when required.
- Failover exercises should preserve allowlist invariants and not cause DNS leaks.
- Latency budget for control plane calls < 50ms median inside same region.

Sketch topology (ASCII) — simplified:

Customer VPC A (model-serving) --(route through)-> Egress VPC (proxy/nat) --(managed egress)-> Internet / Redwood endpoints
                                 |
                                 +--(TGW/Peer)-- On-prem VPN or customer transit

Notes: model-serving subnets have no IGW routes. All outbound goes to Egress VPC via TGW attachments or VPC peering depending on customer preference.

Design options considered (tradeoff summary):
1) Local NAT gateway per AZ + Elastic IPs attached: simple but expensive at scale and slow failover across AZs.
2) Centralized egress VPC with autoscaled proxy fleet (SNAT on instances or eBPF-based forwarder) behind Elastic IP set + HA/Route53 health checks: centralizes IPs and simplifies allowlists, easier to attach interface endpoints to the egress VPC. Single-failure domain mitigated by multi-AZ autoscaled fleet + TGW attachments.
3) Transit/VPN managed egress through customer firewall/NGFW appliance (required by some customers): cost and latency dependent on customer infra; gives strict control but complicates debugging and increases blast radius for outages.

We recommended Option 2 for the POC: centralized egress VPC with a small fixed set of Elastic IPs and a health-aware failover mechanism.

DNS design notes:
- Use split-horizon (private hosted zones) for redwood.internal.customer.example -> private control-plane endpoints (interface endpoints or private IPs in Egress VPC).
- Conditional forwarding/resolver endpoints: AWS Route53 inbound resolver endpoints in customer VPC forward to customer's on-prem DNS where necessary. For Google Cloud / GCP, use Cloud DNS peering or managed forwarding zones.
- Avoid letting model-serving hosts directly query public DNS for redwood-internal names; instead point resolvers to the VPC resolver or use stub resolvers distributed via DHCP options set.
- For external fallback, use a conditional resolver rule that only forwards names under redwood-inference.com to Redwood's public resolver IPs when egress path allows it.

Endpoints / connectivity for Redwood Private control plane:
- Preferred: AWS Interface VPC Endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) from Egress VPC to Redwood Private (if supported in customer region) to keep traffic inside the cloud carrier network. This reduces egress costs and avoids NAT for control-plane calls.
- Fallback: NAT + Elastic IPs with allowlist. Documented list of Control Plane FQDNs used by Redwood (TODO: reconcile with product team).

Security controls and hardening:
- Security groups: only allow outbound 443 from model-serving subnets to egress NAT IPs or the egress proxy SG; egress proxy only allows outbound to Redwood control plane + necessary S3/SecretsManager endpoints.
- IAM: use instance profile roles scoped to minimal privileges; use short-lived credentials for control-plane interactions if possible.
- KMS/HSM: if customer requires, use customer-managed KMS keys for secrets. Documented handshake step for key wrap during bootstrap.

Observability / health checks:
- Active probe from a lightweight worker in model-serving subnet to Redwood control plane endpoints every 10s. Probes reported to a central monitoring dashboard (Datadog).
- Egress fleet publishes health to Route53 health checks; Route53 weighted failover rotates Elastic IPs when a region or AZ is unhealthy.
- Collect traceroutes and connection times to quantify median path latency pre/post change.

Proof-of-concept runbook (happy path):
1) Bootstrap Egress VPC:
   - Create Egress VPC with 3 public subnets (multi-AZ), allocate 4 Elastic IPs (two per AZ), attach autoscaling group of forwarders (nginx/tcp proxy or envoy with NAT).
   - Configure TGW attachment or VPC peering from customer model-serving VPC(s) to Egress VPC.
2) DNS anchor:
   - Create private hosted zone: redwood.internal.customer.example -> record set points to interface endpoint IPs in Egress VPC (or to ALB IPs behind egress fleet).
   - Update DHCP options / resolvers in model-serving VPC to use Route53 resolver endpoints if needed.
3) Endpoint hardening:
   - Create interface endpoints for AWS S3/Secrets Manager/KMS in Egress VPC and add appropriate endpoint policies limiting principals to model-serving role ARNs.
4) Test flows:
   - From a model-serving instance, curl control-plane health endpoint and confirm source IP equals one of Elastic IPs.
   - Kill forwarder in AZ-1 -> observe autoscaling and confirm traffic flows through remaining Elastic IPs; confirm allowlist still valid.
5) Latency and cost capture:
   - Run a 1-hour synthetic token-generation workload and measure p95 latency delta and egress cost delta.

Failure / rollback scenarios:
- If egress fleet becomes unhealthy across all AZs, TGW routes must have an emergency fallback to an alternative egress (on-prem firewall or public internet via IGW) gated by an operator switch. During POC, keep this manual to avoid accidental leaks.
- DNS misconfiguration: restore previous resolver rule via saved Route53 config snapshot.

Open questions / TODOs (customer-specific):
- Which control-plane FQDNs does Redwood expose for Private? (Product needs to finalize.)
- Can customer accept PrivateLink connections to Redwood control plane in their account? If not, we fall back to NAT allowlist.
- How many distinct Elastic IPs can customer accept on their allowlist? This sets autoscaling bounds.
- Customer NGFW vendors: do we need to test application-layer inspection for TLS flows that may break health checks?

Action items (next 2 weeks):
- [Maya] schedule 90-minute workshop with customer network ops to finalize egress IP budget and NGFW inspection policy (Due: 2025-08-20).
- [Arjun] prototype envoy-based forwarder container and publish perf microbenchmarks (Due: 2025-08-22).
- [Lena] create Route53 private zone templates and resolver rule playbook for the POC (Due: 2025-08-18).
- [Diego] open product ticket to provide authoritative list of Redwood Private control-plane hostnames and recommended privateLink configuration (JIRA-ENG-7890).

Quick notes from last workshop:
- Customer network ops insisted on centralized egress for auditability. They prefer interface endpoints over NAT where possible.
- They want an offline-runbook for emergency allowlist rotation (we should script this as an IaC module).

Appendix: quick envoy forwarder config (sketch) — use host networking or privileged cap_net_raw for direct SNAT: 
- Upstream: TLS passthrough to control-plane FQDNs
- Health: /healthz endpoint on 9000 returning 200 when DNS resolution and TLS handshake succeed
